quote: In weiter Ferne taucht dann einmal das Problem auf alle nicht auflösbaren Gleichungen 5ten Grades mit vorgeschriebener Diskriminante zu construiren.
english: In the far distance there then appears the problem of constructing all non-solvable equations of the 5th degree with prescribed discriminant.
topic: Short notes on constructing all non-solvable quintic equations with prescribed discriminant, on when continuation of potentials is permitted, and remarks on the critical period in mathematics and on general theories.

triage.modern_statement: Given a discriminant D, find all quintic polynomials over Q that are not solvable by radicals, i.e. whose Galois group is A5 or S5, and that have discriminant D. Polynomial discriminants change by square factors when the polynomial is transformed, so the natural modern version is about fields: for a given D, list all quintic number fields K with disc(K) = D whose Galois closure has group S5 or A5, and give a defining polynomial for each. Hermite's theorem guarantees there are only finitely many such fields, so the real question is how to construct or enumerate them effectively. Related questions ask how many such fields there are with |D| ≤ X.
triage.answered_by: No single person resolved this; it was settled step by step. Hermite (and Minkowski) proved that only finitely many number fields have a given discriminant, which makes the problem finite in principle. Hunter–Pohst-style geometry-of-numbers searches then made it computable. Schwarz, Pohst and Diaz y Diaz (Math. Comp. 63, 1994) listed all quintic fields with |disc| below set bounds, e.g. 2×10^7 for totally real fields. Bhargava (Annals of Math., 2010) parametrized quintic rings and counted quintic fields by discriminant, showing that 100% of them have Galois group S5. Jones and Roberts built an online database of number fields (LMS J. Comput. Math. 17, 2014). Together, these let anyone find every quintic field, including the non-solvable ones, for any given discriminant.

evidence.claim: Hermite's theorem: only finitely many number fields have bounded discriminant. Exactly how many there are is still described as an open problem.
Schwarz, Pohst and Diaz y Diaz (Math. Comp. 63, 1994) enumerated all degree-5 fields up to discriminant bounds, e.g. 2×10^7 for totally real fields.
Bhargava found the asymptotic density of quintic field discriminants and showed that 100% of quintic fields ordered by discriminant have Galois group S5.
Jones and Roberts describe an online database of number fields that includes quintic fields listed by discriminant and ramification.

triage.why: Hilbert's remark matches what is now called enumerating quintic number fields by discriminant and Galois group. It is not one of his 23 published problems or the 24th problem. Hermite's finiteness theorem makes it a finite problem, and geometry-of-numbers algorithms with published tables (Schwarz–Pohst–Diaz y Diaz 1994) and databases (Jones–Roberts) make it practically solvable for any given discriminant. Bhargava's 2010 work answers the related counting question. Research continues on asymptotic counts and on fields with prescribed ramification, so the area is still active. Confidence is medium for three reasons. Hilbert's wording is brief, so 'construct all' could mean an explicit parametrization rather than an algorithm, and that sense has no clean answer. I found no source linking this notebook entry to later work, so the identification is my own. And I did not confirm that the sources contain a statement of an explicit, general algorithm for a single fixed discriminant.
